Scaling Linear’s GTM to $100M ARR — Cristina Cordova, COO 
>50% of tickets written by agents, the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR, and selling without SDRs or FDEs

Listen to this conversation 84 min 
Read transcript Watch on YouTube 
On this page ⌄ Half the work on Linear is now created by agents "Issue tracking is dead" The AI budget behind $100M in months Linear threw out its 2025 enterprise roadmap No SDRs, no forward deployed engineers Everyone wants outcome-based pricing Why not hire 100 salespeople? Show notes Timestamps Transcript Thanks for reading 
Open video on YouTube ↗ 
Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova , COO of Linear , about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. 
Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. 
When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation . 
We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. 
Half the work on Linear is now created by agents 
Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. 
That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. 
So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs and app usage doesn't, you're becoming a commodity. At Linear, both are up and to the right, because people still come back to the app to see and coordinate the work. 
Jump to the MCP discussion → 
"Issue tracking is dead" 
When Karri published "Issue tracking is dead" in March, most of Linear's customers agreed with him. Then they asked the obvious question: so what am I buying? Linear's answer is a product development system built around agent orchestration, where humans stop doing the manual work of filing, labeling, assigning and closing issues. 
Customers had been pushing it there. Most of the frontier AI labs run on Linear and wanted it to move faster. Pre-AI companies like Ramp and Coinbase were building their own internal agents and needed an API to plug them into Linear. 
Cristina says Linear is lucky it's small enough to cannibalize itself. Google has a much harder problem: put an AI answer above every search result, and fewer people look at the ads. 
Jump to the "issue tracking is dead" discussion → 
The AI budget behind $100M in months 
The thing speeding up purchases right now, Cristina says, is AI budget. Companies carved out money for AI tools that didn't exist before, and any product that fits inside it skips the usual fight for spend. At some companies that budget is very high. 
It's already starting to change. Buyers are signing one-year deals and paid pilots, not three-year contracts, because nobody knows what they'll want in two years. And some overnight-$100M stories are a handful of $30 to $40 million contracts with defense companies or giant law firms. That's a very different business from Linear's 40,000 paying customers on what was, until June, entirely seat-based pricing. 
When those one-year deals come up for renewal, we'll find out whose ARR was real. 
Jump to the AI budget discussion → 
Linear threw out its 2025 enterprise roadmap 
Three weeks after joining in 2023, Cristina crossed "move upmarket to enterprise" off Linear's company goals. It had one salesperson. She went after growth-stage companies that would have to rip out an existing tool instead, the same way Stripe won new businesses long before it won switchers. 
Linear finally declared an enterprise push in 2025, with a roadmap full of features for large organizations. Then agents happened. Linear built an MCP server, an agents platform with a whole new set of APIs, and integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot. None of it was planned, and a lot of the enterprise work never got done. 
Cristina chose to race ahead anyway. Competitors waited, and enterprises started putting Linear on their shortlists. 
Jump to the enterprise roadmap discussion → 
No SDRs, no forward deployed engineers 
Linear has never hired a single SDR. Cristina thinks the qualification call wastes the customer's time: they want a demo, not questions about their budget. AEs do their own outbound, with tooling to keep it personal. 
It doesn't do forward deployed engineering either. Linear should be easy enough to adopt that nobody needs access to your systems. Solutions engineers sell alongside enterprise AEs instead, sometimes building a working ServiceNow integration overnight to show a prospect it can be done. Cristina adds that an opinionated tool gives agents cleaner data than one where every team defines "bug" differently. 
Support stays in-house, and Linear won't let an LLM answer tickets on its own. AI drafts replies and a human decides what goes out. Customers sometimes assume the replies are AI because they arrive so fast. In three and a half years, Cristina has never had an escalation over a bad support experience. 
Jump to the sales team discussion → 
Everyone wants outcome-based pricing 
Cristina would love a model like Intercom's Fin, which charges for each support conversation its AI resolves. It's harder for Linear. What is auto-triaging a bug to the right team worth when one company thinks that's the PM's job and another doesn't? 
Until someone cracks that, Linear charges for what costs it money and keeps the rest free. Seats stay. Linear Agent chat is free even though it runs on frontier models. In coding sessions, users pick OpenAI or Anthropic models and harnesses, and Linear passes through the published API price plus a small markup. Loops run on AI credits. 
Linear doesn't start charging for things that used to be free. New AI features launch as free betas with notice that pricing is coming, and prices start high and come down rather than the other way around. 
Jump to the pricing discussion → 
Why not hire 100 salespeople? 
Cristina says Linear runs on about half the headcount of companies at its stage and revenue. A sales team bigger than the rest of the company would have cost it the trust engineering now has in sales. 
From Stripe she brought a 40% rule: at least 40% of the company should be engineering, product, design and data. If sales wanted more people, it helped recruit engineers first. Linear has no hard rule, but one of the first things she built was a headcount spreadsheet by function, and she still watches the ratio. 
Hiring is slow on purpose. Candidates do a work trial on a real problem. Hers was writing Linear's go-to-market plan for the next six to twelve months, which then became her job. At about 170 people, the only C-suite is the founders and her. 
Jump to the hiring discussion →

podcasts.title: Gemini and the path to AGI with Koray Kavukcuoglu
podcasts.description:
Seven years after their last conversation at Google DeepMind’s London office, Professor Hannah Fry reunites with Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP of Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect at Google. Back then, DeepMind was focused on specialized breakthroughs like AlphaGo and AlphaFold; today, Koray is leading the charge toward general-purpose intelligence with Gemini. In this episode, they discuss why real-world products are essential to building AGI, how Gemini’s architecture continuously evolves, and the topic on everyone's mind: recursive self-improvement. Join Professor Hannah Fry as she uncovers the extraordinary way AI is transforming our world 
2025 
2024 
Past episodes 
2025 
Our latest conversations with Hannah Fry 
Slide 1 of 10 
2025, Episode 10 
Part 2: Social engineering, malware, and the future of cybersecurity in AI 
In part two, Hannah and Four tackle the human element at the heart of cybersecurity: Who are the bad actors, and what motivates them? They dissect the evolving strategies designed to stop social engineering attacks - like passkeys and risk-based authentication - and confront the complex security and privacy challenges that may be introduced by autonomous agents. 
2025, Episode 9 
Part 1: Social engineering, malware, and the future of cybersecurity in AI 
Hannah Fry and Four Flynn take us behind the scenes of Operation Aurora, the monumental 2009 attack on Google that forever changed the landscape of cybersecurity. They discuss the defender's dilemma, the constant battle between attackers and defenders in the digital world, and how AI can potentially help mitigate some of the most complex vulnerabilities. 
2025, Episode 8 
Genie 3: An infinite world model with Shlomi Fruchter and Jack Parker-Holder 
In this episode, Professor Hannah Fry speaks with Jack Parker-Holder and Shlomi Fruchter about Genie 3, a general-purpose world model that can generate an unprecedented diversity of interactive environments. The conversation covers how this model's auto-regressive nature allows for the creation of consistent, explorable worlds from text or image prompts, and how its capabilities differ from video generation models like Veo. 
2025, Episode 7 
A whistle stop tour of AI creation with Paige Bailey 
This week's episode is a slight departure from our usual deep dives. Join Paige Bailey, DevRel lead, as she guides Hannah Fry though some of her favorite AI tools. Having spent years understanding the 'what' of these models, Hannah finally gets to experience the 'how’ – from generating prompts and 'vibe coding', to creating her own version of the infamous spaghetti meme. 
2025, Episode 6 
The nature of AI: solving the planet's data gap with Drew Purves 
Could we use the sound of a coral reef to determine its health? Do we know where all the world's natural forests are? And are we on the verge of using AI to decode animal communication? In this episode, Professor Hannah Fry is joined by Drew Purves, Nature Lead at Google DeepMind. They explore how AI is helping ecologists map forests and species for the first time in history and how this data can be used to better understand the root causes of deforestation. 
2025, Episode 5 
A quest for a cure: AI drug design with Isomorphic Labs 
In this episode, host Hannah Fry is joined by Max Jaderberg and Rebecca Paul of Isomorphic Labs to explore the future of drug discovery in the age of AI. They discuss how new technology, particularly AlphaFold 3, is revolutionizing the field by predicting the structure of life’s molecules, paving the way for faster and more efficient drug discovery. 
2025, Episode 4 
Redefining robotics with Carolina Parada 
On this episode, Hannah is joined by Carolina Parada, Senior Director and Head of Robotics at Google DeepMind. They explore the recent leap forward in robotic capabilities, highlighting advancements in multimodal understanding and embodied reasoning, which enable robots to interact with the physical world with unprecedented generality. 
2025, Episode 3 
AI and the future of health with Joelle Barral 
In this episode, Professor Hannah Fry interviews Joelle Barral, Senior Director of Research at Google DeepMind, about AI in healthcare. They discuss existing AI applications including image analysis for diabetic retinopathy and the expansion of diagnostic tools as a result of multi-modal models. The conversation highlights AI's potential to improve healthcare delivery, personalize treatment, expand access worldwide, and ultimately, bring back the joy of practicing medicine. 
2025, Episode 2 
Consciousness, reasoning and the philosophy of AI with Murray Shanahan 
In this episode, Hannah is once again joined by Murray Shanahan, Professor of Cognitive Robotics at Imperial College London and Principal Scientist at Google DeepMind, for a philosophical deep dive on AI. They explore everything from consciousness and metacognition in animals, to symbolic AI and neural networks. Murray also
s insights into his involvement with the film 'Ex Machina' and discusses the idea of reasoning, anthropomorphism, and the future of AI. 
2025, Episode 1 
Is human data enough? With David Silver 
In this episode of Google DeepMind: The Podcast, VP of Reinforcement Learning, David Silver, describes his vision for the future of AI, exploring the concept of the "era of experience" versus the current "era of human data". Using AlphaGo and AlphaZero as examples, he highlights how these systems surpassed human capabilities by engaging in reinforcement learning without prior human knowledge. This approach contrasts with large language models, which depend on human data and feedback. Silver emphasizes the need to explore this path to drive AI progress and achieve artificial superintelligence. 
2024 
Slide 1 of 13 
2024, Episode 12 
Project Astra: Exploring a Universal AI Assistant with Greg Wayne 
In our final episode for the year, we explore Project Astra, a research prototype exploring future capabilities of a universal AI assistant that can understand the world around you. Host Hannah Fry is joined by Greg Wayne, Director in Research at Google DeepMind. They discuss the inspiration behind the research prototype, its current strengths and limitations, as well as potential future use cases. Hannah even gets the chance to put Project Astra's multilingual skills to the test. 
2024, Episode 11 
Gemini 2.0 and the evolution of agentic AI with Oriol Vinyals 
In this episode, Hannah is joined by Oriol Vinyals, VP of Drastic Research and Gemini co-lead. They discuss the evolution of agents from single-task models to more general-purpose models capable of broader applications, like Gemini. Vinyals guides Hannah through the two-step process behind multi modal models: pre-training (imitation learning) and post-training (reinforcement learning). They discuss the complexities of scaling and the importance of innovation in architecture and training processes. They close on a quick whirlwind tour of some of the new agentic capabilities recently released by Google DeepMind. 
2024, Episode 10 
The Balancing Act: Regulation & AI with Nicklas Lundblad 
There is broad consensus across the tech industry, governments and society, that as artificial intelligence becomes more embedded in every aspect of our world, regulation is essential. But what does regulation look like? Can it be adopted without stifling innovation? Are current frameworks presented by government leaders enough? 
Join host Hannah Fry as she discusses these questions and more with Nicklas Lundblad, director of Public Policy at Google DeepMind. 
2024, Episode 9 
Inside NotebookLM with Raiza Martin and Steven Johnson 
NotebookLM is a research assistant powered by Gemini that draws on expertise from storytelling to present information in an engaging way. It allows users to upload their own documents and generate insights, explanations, and—more recently—podcasts. This innovative feature has captured the imagination of millions of people worldwide, who have created thousands of engaging podcasts ranging from personal narratives to educational explainers using source materials like CVs, personal journals, sales decks, and more. 
2024, Bonus Episode 
AI for Science with Sir Paul Nurse, Demis Hassabis, Jennifer Doudna, and John Jumper 
Join Professor Hannah Fry at the AI for Science Forum for a fascinating conversation with Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis. They explore how AI is revolutionizing scientific discovery, delving into topics like the nuclear pore complex, plastic-eating enzymes, quantum computing, and the power of Turing machines. The episode also features a special 'ask me anything' session with Nobel Laureates Sir Paul Nurse, Jennifer Doudna, and John Jumper, who answer audience questions about the future of AI in science. 
2024, Episode 8 
The Ethics of AI Assistants with Iason Gabriel 
In this episode, host Hannah Fry and DeepMind Research Scientist Iason Gabriel discuss the ethical implications of advanced AI assistants. Drawing from Iason's recent paper, they examine value alignment, anthropomorphism, safety concerns, and the potential societal impact of these technologies. 
2024, Episode 7 
AI in the classroom with Irina Jurenka 
How human should an AI tutor be? What does ‘good’ teaching look like? Will AI lead in the classroom, or take a back seat to human instruction? Will everyone have their own personalized AI tutor? Join Research Lead, Irina Jurenka, and Professor Hannah Fry as they explore the complicated yet exciting world of AI in education. 
2024, Episode 6 
AI: Supercharging Scientific Exploration with Pushmeet Kohli 
In this episode, Professor Hannah Fry sits down with Pushmeet Kohli, VP of Research at Google DeepMind to discuss AI’s impact on scientific discovery. They go on a whirlwind tour of scientific projects, touching on recent breakthroughs in material science, biology, weather forecasting, and mathematics to better understand how AI can enhance our scientific understanding of the world. 
2024, Episode 5 
Gaming, Goats & General Intelligence with Frederic Besse 
Games are a very good training ground for agents. Think about it. Perfectly packaged, neatly constrained environments where agents can run wild, work out the rules for themselves, and learn how to handle autonomy. In this episode, Research Engineering Team Lead, Frederic Besse, joins Hannah as they discuss important research like SIMA (Scalable Instructable Multiworld Agent) and what we can expect from future agents that can understand and safely carry out a wide range of tasks - online and in the real world. 
2024, Episode 4 
Decoding Google Gemini with Jeff Dean 
Professor Hannah Fry is joined by Jeff Dean, one of the most legendary figures in computer science and chief scientist of Google DeepMind and Google Research. Jeff was instrumental to the field in the late 1990s, writing the code that transformed Google from a small startup into the multinational company it is today. Hannah and Jeff discuss it all - from the early days of Google and neural networks, to the long term potential of multi-modal models like Gemini. 
2024, Episode 3 
AI Safety... Ok Doomer: with Anca Dragan 
Building safe and capable models is one of the greatest challenges of our time. Can we make AI work for everyone? How do we prevent existential threats? Why is alignment so important? Join Professor Hannah Fry as she delves into these critical questions with Anca Dragan, lead for AI safety and alignment at Google DeepMind. 
2024, Episode 2 
AI: Your New Creative Muse? with Douglas Eck 
In this episode, Professor Hannah Fry and Google DeepMind's senior research director Doug Eck explore AI's capacity for true creativity. They delve into the complexities of defining creativity, the challenges of AI generated content and attribution, and whether AI can help us to connect with each other in new and meaningful ways. 
2024, Episode 1 
Unreasonably Effective AI with Demis Hassabis 
It has been a few years since Google DeepMind CEO and co-founder, Demis Hassabis, and Professor Hannah Fry caught up, and in that time, the world has caught on to artificial intelligence—in a big way. Listen in as they discuss the recent explosion of interest in AI, what Demis means when he describes chatbots as ‘unreasonably effective’, and the unexpected emergence of capabilities like conceptual understanding and abstraction in recent generative models.

podcasts.title: How Fast Should We Build Superintelligence? | Nick Bostrom
podcasts.description:
The question isn’t simply whether humanity should race toward superintelligence or stop. Nick Bostrom argues the harder challenge is preserving the ability to slow down when safety falls behind, without turning a temporary pause into permanent technological stagnation.

a16z’s Eddy Lazzarin and Elena Burger sit down with Bostrom to revisit the ideas he helped bring into the mainstream, now that increasingly capable AI systems actually exist. They discuss why alignment may become harder as models grow more situationally aware, which capability improvements may carry more risk than others, and why Bostrom favors “pacing the frontier” rather than committing to a broad or indefinite pause.

They also examine the cost of waiting. Bostrom argues that safely developed superintelligence could radically extend human lifespans and address problems from disease to poverty, meaning delay carries risks of its own. From there, the conversation turns to Deep Utopia, governance, the possibility of post-human forms of life, the simulation argument, and whether AI could eventually surpass humans at philosophy itself.

podcasts.title: Superintelligence Needs the Physical World with CEO and Co-Founder of Arda Bob McGrew
podcasts.description:
Is the AI singularity actually coming? Bob McGrew, former Chief Research Officer at OpenAI, argues that superintelligence won’t arrive without changes in the physical world, and that the “hard takeoff” argument is wrong.

Sarah Guo and Elad Gil sit down with Bob, an early key executive at Palantir who later led research at OpenAI. He is now CEO and co-founder of Arda, which is leveraging AI to make American manufacturing competitive. Bob explains why automating AI researchers is a one-time boost rather than a runaway loop, and why GPUs, compute, wet labs, and factories are the real bottlenecks. 

They cover Arda’s work with Anduril on everything from actuators to missiles to the Fury combat aircraft, why Arda is building “Cursor for manufacturing engineers”, and how the forward deployed engineering model really works. Plus, the big-picture future view: machines that make machines, self-replicating factories, and Bob’s answer to the Fermi paradox.

Sign up for new podcasts every week. Email feedback to show@no-priors.com

Follow us on Twitter: @NoPriorsPod | @Saranormous | @EladGil | @bobmcgrewai | @Arda_Industries

Chapters:

00:00 – Trailer

00:05 – Bob McGrew Introduction

01:05 – Why work on the physical world during the AI revolution?

podcasts.title: Evolution of Digital Assets at Grayscale – Peter Mintzberg (EP.528)
podcasts.description:
Peter Mintzberg is CEO of Grayscale, one of the world's largest digital asset managers founded in 2013.

 
 
Peter joined Grayscale two years ago after a career in strategy and M&A at Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and BlackRock. He saw digital assets as the next step in the evolution of traditional finance.
 
 
Our conversation covers the rapid mainstream adoption of digital assets, Grayscale's transition from its pioneering trusts to a broad ETF platform, and opportunities beyond Bitcoin and Ethereum. We discuss active management in digital assets, the evolution of blockchain applications, and the changing regulatory environment.
 
 
We then turn to Peter's view of what comes next, including the convergence of AI and tokenization, personalized portfolios, and a future where the distinction between liquid and illiquid assets fades away.
 
 
See full disclaimer here.

Gemini 4 Neon: GDM's Opus/Sol Contender 
November 18, 2026 — Google’s middle tier scores 61 on the Intelligence Index. Plus, Anthropic prices its IPO at $83. 
swyx .ai 
Nov 18 · 7 min read
Google DeepMind shipped Gemini 4 Neon , its fourth Gemini 4 model in about seven weeks. If you’re confused about the naming, you’re not alone; the 1.5 month old Argon is now retired , the old Pro and Flash from Gemini 1-3 are dead, and if you’re thinking the names are based on atomic weights, Neon (10), the midtier model is faster/cheaper than Carbon (6). This is a helpful guide to the current leading models and sizes: 
Because of how distillation, RL, and benchmarking works, Neon technically outperforms Carbon by some measures despite being a smaller model… 
Also today, Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per
, above its initial range, and Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy Applied Compute in a $4.5B all-stock deal . Anthropic · Palo Alto Networks 
AI News for November 17–18, 2026. We checked 12 subreddits and 544 Twitter accounts . Browse past issues . 
AI Twitter Recap 
Gemini 4 Neon 
Launch and availability 
Pricing and specs. Neon costs $3 for input, $0.15 for cached input and $15 for output per million tokens. It has a 1M-token context window and four effort levels. Vals reports a maximum output limit of 1M tokens. Google · Vals 
Rollout. Neon is coming to the paid Gemini API in AI Studio and Android Studio, Gemini for business, and Antigravity for Pro and Ultra
rs. In the Gemini app, Pro and Ultra users can select it as “Deeper analysis,” including for Tasks. Google’s rollout · Gemini app 
Day-one integrations. Cursor , GitHub Copilot across its app, CLI and VS Code, and LangChain Managed Deep Agents . 
Release cadence. Arena counted gaps of 28 days between Argon and Carbon, 15 between Carbon and Hydrogen, and six between Hydrogen and Neon. Arena 
Independent results 
High versus xhigh. At high effort, Neon matched Carbon’s 60 on the Intelligence Index for $3.74 per task. On GDP.pdf it scored 33.4% at high and 28.0% at xhigh. Artificial Analysis 
Agent Arena. Neon debuted second with 1,336 points across about 4,200 sessions. It had a $2.82 median task cost and placed second on steerability. Carbon still leads the separate Text Arena. Agent Arena · Text Arena 
Vals. Neon placed second on the Vals Index at 70.9%, about 0.4 points behind Fable 5.2 at less than half the cost per task. On Code Migration it averaged 160 turns, fewer than Carbon’s 234 or Hydrogen’s 574, and scored below both. Vals Index · Code Migration 
CursorBench 4.1. Neon scored 63.7% at default effort, up from Hydrogen’s 57.3%. Cursor 
Hands-on reports 
Steering and capacity. In 13 early Antigravity sessions, Kimmonismus recorded 762 tool calls and a 93% input-cache hit rate. When told to avoid the terminal, Neon ran zero shell commands in those tests. The logs also recorded 57 capacity errors and four stalled runs. Test logs 
How teams use it. Theo says he’s now using Neon for copy, Fable to implement changes, and Astra to playtest. Jeremy Howard praised Neon while saying he was reverting Solveit’s Astra and Sol options to their pre-6.2 versions. Theo · Jeremy Howard 
New results for GPT-6.2 
Math and formal proof. Astra and Sol took the top two spots on MathArena. Astra solved 42 of 53 ArXivLean problems. Vals separately reports what it believes is the first formalization in Lean of Smoktunowicz’s Gap Theorem, with the proof checked by an independent kernel replay. Tim Gehr · Vals 
Agent Arena. Astra debuted sixth. Sol placed eleventh at a $0.90 median task cost. On the separate Code Arena WebDev board, Astra placed third at a 42% lower median cost than its predecessor. Agent Arena · WebDev 
Background discounts. OpenAI opened a public beta for GPT-6.2 Responses API jobs that can wait. Two-hour and eight-hour targets for the first response come with 30% and 40% discounts per token, respectively. OpenAI Developers 
What changed after launch. OpenAI’s Tibo Sottiaux says early reviewers used builds from before the final few days of changes. Artificial Analysis found Astra’s responses got shorter and it was less likely to admit uncertainty in its behavioral evaluation. Sottiaux · Artificial Analysis 
Sponsored Your sponsor ad here Reach the AI engineers building what comes next. 
Latent Space is read by the people shipping agents, models and infrastructure. Enquire about sponsoring this slot. 
business@latent.space → 
Open weights and inference 
Correction to yesterday’s Pi adapter numbers. Yesterday’s issue cited 15 to 32 solves on the 51 hardest SWE-bench Pro tasks. Hugging Face reran affected tasks after finding a tunnel outage that hit nine base-model runs. The corrected result is 20 to 33 solves , or 39.2% to 64.7%. It also released an OpenCode adapter that moved Qwen3.8-27B from 35.3% to 51.0% on the same subset with thinking off. Corrected model card · OpenCode release 
Tencent releases Hy4 Flash weights. The 224B-parameter multimodal MoE activates 12B parameters per token, supports 1M context and includes a roughly 64B n-gram embedding table. Tencent released instruct, FP8 and base checkpoints. Tencent repository · vLLM 
vLLM 0.34.0. The extensible KV cache is on by default and Model Runner V2 is the sole GPU runner. The team reports up to 1.95× faster NVFP4 decoding on GB200. vLLM 
Inference capacity grew faster than peak compute. Epoch estimates that the capacity of chips sold for a fixed basket of agent workloads grew 4.6× from Q2 2025 to Q2 2026, while peak 8-bit compute grew 2.6×. Epoch AI 
Runway cuts serving hardware in half. It reports serving a 57B video model at 24 fps on four GPUs, down from eight. Runway 
Agent tooling. Prime Intellect launched Model Factory for RL, supervised fine-tuning, serving and evals. Hugging Face released the message dataset from its 1,000-agent PyBot project. Prime Intellect · Hugging Face 
Research and chip design 
OpenAI models help redesign AMD circuits. OpenAI reports up to 14% improvement against optimized baselines on blocks of AMD’s flagship GPU design. The team used Synopsys tools to check that rewritten circuits preserved behavior and to measure power, performance and area. Some changes made it into a design sent for manufacturing. OpenAI 
Measuring research acceleration. OpenAI published an update on internal agent use and research task completion, and proposed regular disclosure of indicators for AI research acceleration. OpenAI 
Smaller harness edits can save tokens. In a 40-issue held-out test, a gated approach that edited one module at a time scored 40.0% on SWE-bench Lite at 46.7K tokens per task. A full rewrite scored 42.5% at 451.6K tokens. DAIR research summary 
Agent teamwork. MAC Bench finds most gains from eight agents came from exploring in parallel. Opus 5.5 was the sole tested model to show an added gain from coordination. Bespoke Labs 
Media and voice 
Genie 4 reaches Project Genie. Google’s world model adds native audio and lets users change the world with text mid-session. Access is rolling out to eligible Google AI Ultra
rs. Google DeepMind 
Turn detection and transcription. Inworld released weights for a voice-isolation model and its SAVA turn detector, which it says detects completed turns in a median 71 ms. AssemblyAI split its 3.7 release into models for voice agents, live transcription and recordings. Inworld · AssemblyAI 
Kling Image 4.0. It placed seventh in Artificial Analysis’s text-to-image rankings and sixth in editing. Artificial Analysis 
Industry 
Anthropic prices its IPO at $83. The offering covers 980M
s, about $81.3B at the offer price. About $79.4B of that comes from
s sold by Anthropic before fees. Nasdaq trading under ANT is expected November 19. Anthropic 
Palo Alto Networks agrees to buy Applied Compute. The $4.5B all-stock deal gives Palo Alto a platform for post-training and serving open-weight models. The companies expect to close in Palo Alto’s fiscal Q3 2027, subject to regulatory clearance and other conditions. Palo Alto Networks 
AI Reddit Recap 
Local audio 
Blue TTS v3. A developer says their MIT-licensed model generates audio at about 50× real time on CPU. The thread’s headline number is a throughput claim about that setup. Code and demos · Discussion 
Inworld voice isolation. The release includes a 64M-parameter model for offline use and a 58M model for real-time use, both at 48 kHz. Weights · Local tests and discussion 
AudioGhost. A local interface for Meta’s SAM-Audio lets users describe a sound in text and separate it from the rest of a recording. Project discussion 
Local inference and coding 
Experts from an SSD. TokenWing’s developer claims it can stream a majority of routed experts from SSD. A user reported 45–50 tok/s on a 120B MoE with 12 GB of VRAM and 32 GB of RAM. LocalLLM thread

Introduction 
Lex Fridman (00:00:00) The following is a conversation with Larry Lawton, one of the most notorious and prolific jewelry thieves in US history, who was eventually caught by the FBI, spent more than a decade in prison, including a lot of time in the hole, and then he turned his life around to run the Reality Check program that helps keep at-risk youth out of prison. He now hosts a YouTube channel where he breaks down real crimes, prison life, and how realistic the heists in movies and video games are with, of course, a lot of focus on Grand Theft Auto 3, 4, 5, and now GTA 6. This conversation is in two parts. The first part we recorded just now focused on GTA 6 and some other recent topics. 
Lex Fridman (00:00:52) The second part we recorded a while back, and it tells the timeless story of his life, the heists, the mob, the prison time, and what it takes to rebuild a life after losing everything. In this conversation and in general, Larry holds nothing back: sex, violence, drugs, robberies, all of it. He is also, in the time I’ve known him, a truly kind human being, which to me is a humbling glimpse into the complexity of human nature and the paths each of us can take in life and the evolution each of us can go through in life. This is the Lex Fridman Podcast. To support it, please check out our sponsors in the description where you can also find links to contact me, ask questions, give feedback, and so on. And now, dear friends, here’s Larry Lawton. 
Lex Fridman (00:01:41) All right. 
GTA 6 
Lex Fridman (00:01:46) For people who don’t know, you were one of the most prolific, notorious jewelry thieves in US history. You were arrested by the FBI, served your time in prison, and since then you’ve done a lot of good for the community helping at-risk youth. And we’ll talk about your life, we’ll talk about your history, we’ll talk about the whole journey in prison, but first we’ve gotta talk about GTA 6. 
Larry Lawton (00:02:08) I’m an open book, Lex, you know that. And I’m glad to be here. You know, I think you do great work, and I think this is gonna be great- … because you played the game. 
Lex Fridman (00:02:17) Yeah, I played in terms of Grand Theft Auto, I played GTA 1, GTA 2, 3, Vice City, 4, and 5. The world that they created is bigger than life. A lot of the things that we love about movies, a lot of the things we love about video games. And I think in terms of GTA 6, in terms of places that are bigger than life, I mean, Miami, South Florida, this is your stomping ground. Like, how does that feel that Grand Theft Auto 6, likely the biggest game of all time by far, is set in this place where you operated as a jewelry thief? 
Larry Lawton (00:02:54) It’s… I’m going crazy. When I found out, what happened was I- 
Lex Fridman (00:02:58) You’re basically a GTA 6 character, Larry. 
Larry Lawton (00:03:01) Yeah. I mean, it’s kinda crazy that way because I didn’t know what GTA was really. I heard of it like everybody else. But I got into it, and it’s really amazing. I got into it so much, I’d lose my head in this game. And then I kept thinking what I would do in this game, what I would do. And that’s what made me start really thinking more about GTA and the game and the crimes, ’cause that’s what I did. My headquarters was down there in Mia… I started that… Well, my first robbery was in South Florida. It was a setup. But the game, I’m dying to see how they really portray an actual robbery, the actual how much they use for the casing. 
Larry Lawton (00:03:45) I’ve cased stores for two weeks, and I’ve cased stores for six weeks. You know, I mean, it could take forever to case a store. And I knew everything about a store. And if they wanna do a robbery right, they have to do it from when is the mailman coming, when is packages delivering, when is the sun setting, sun rising, so you could see the glare in the windows. There’s so many variables that go into a robbery. And, you know, being I did so many, probably 25 or more, and, you know, I robbed so many that I had to travel up the East Coast to keep robbing. And I couldn’t rob in New York because of affiliations with organized crime. They’re protected. 
Larry Lawton (00:04:23) You know, you don’t just go into a store in New York and rob it, especially my day in the ’90s, ’80s and ’90s, because what happened then, it’s protected by the mob. They get protection. And once they find out who did it, there’s no calling the police. 
Lex Fridman (00:04:38) And you worked for the mob in New York? 
Larry Lawton (00:04:41) Yeah, I was associated with the Gambino crime family, and made a lot of money for a lot of people. I had my fence there. I had my people there. I would go in, Lex, with a bag of diamonds worth million dollars, put ’em on a table. When I robbed the jewelry store, I didn’t just rob a little bit. I robbed the whole store. There wasn’t anything left. And it was funny because the government said… You know, I was arrested by a guy named Matt Mullen in FBI. Nice guy, too. I ended up talking to him. He ended up passing away about a year ago, maybe a little more. And he was really good. He goes, “I got you.” You know, he goes, “I was looking for you for six years.” And it’s funny because I didn’t know that, of course. 
Larry Lawton (00:05:25) I didn’t know that they would flood an area with FBI agents after I did a robbery, the kind of MO I did. And they ended up getting me on great police work. So if anybody says the FBI’s stupid, run from ’em. Don’t walk from ’em, ’cause they’re wrong. 
Lex Fridman (00:05:43) So you did a lot of right things to make sure you don’t get caught, and you’re saying they did a good job of figuring it out. 
Larry Lawton (00:05:50) You know, it took them so long time, six years. And I robbed so many stores. The guy said, “You’re the best I’ve ever seen do it.” And I don’t know if that… I don’t wanna sound like I’m bragging about crime. 
Larry Lawton (00:06:02) It’s weird, ’cause now I look at that, and I lost a lot of my life. I lost my kids. You know, not good. I have a good relationship with my kids, and my son was just turned seven. He was born November 30th. I got arrested December 2nd, and he turned seven, and my daughter was 15 months old. And my daughter’s in Miami and I see her. My son is in Brooklyn, I see him. No, he now moved to Staten Island. Moved up in the world. That’s what we used to call it back in Brooklyn. You know, you go from the Bronx to Brooklyn to Staten Island or something like that, you’re moving up in the world. And so it’s kinda wild. And now I help people, so I look at it like… I look at robberies all the time. 
Larry Lawton (00:06:48) I mean, I can walk down a street to this day, and I don’t care with security cameras and stuff, and I could tell you if I could rob that store, and I could tell you how to do it. And whenever I do, people look and says, “Oh my God, you are 100% right.” And it’s just the little things. It’s people. You’re not robbing technology, you’re robbing people. And when people make mistakes. 
Lex Fridman (00:07:12) So you’re saying with all the extra technology we have in the world, with all the cameras, with all the surveillance, with all of that, you’re still, it’s still about the people? 
Larry Lawton (00:07:19) Absolutely. You know as well as I do, technology you can maneuver. You can stop cameras. There’s people who know how to do a lot of that. I’m not even talking about that. I’m talking about people. People are habit driven, so what they’ll do is they’ll go to work in the same way every time, and I’ll know, so I’ll know exactly when they come in, when they come out, who’s there. Even going down to the postal, and you’re going down to deliveries on FedEx or UPS, they come at a certain time in certain areas, and you get to know that. So I know who’s coming and going in that store, and I know who the neighbor is of that store. 
Larry Lawton (00:07:56) And I always robbed in strip malls where there’s usually anchored by a big store like a supermarket, like Publix as in South Florida or Winn-Dixie, and they usu- So you could case that store by sitting in a car reading a paper, like your paper, and you’re really watching the store. So it’s a whole different thing when you, when you’re doing it for real. And I’m dying, I really am, wanting to see how Rockstar did it. 
Lex Fridman (00:08:22) So a big part of it, and you hope to see that in the game, is casing. So doing the research, um- 
Larry Lawton (00:08:28) Research. What I heard about in the game, now they’re gonna make it where everything is interactive. Like, Jason can make a decision and it goes one way. Lucia can make a decision and go another way. This is what I’m hearing. If that is true, who’s gonna make that decision when… Is it gonna be a, “Oh, he just cased it”? ‘Cause if you just walk into a jewelry store, you’re done. Let’s end the game. Let’s shoot him and get another character, because he’s not gonna make it. He’s gonna be arrested. There’s no question in my mind. I watch guys think, “Oh, I can rob a jewelry store.” Next thing you know, they write me from prison. 
Lex Fridman (00:09:00) So what’s the… Casing is understanding all the technology, understanding the, the time of day when certain things happen, understanding the people that are working there, the weak points, the security guards, all that. So all those components. 
Larry Lawton (00:09:12) Yeah, more, even more than that. It could be where the neighbors are, who’s gonna walk by, when the sun is rising, and when it’s setting so there’s glare on the window. Every aspect beforehand of planning that robbery with things that can make you get caught is part of casing. 
Lex Fridman (00:09:29) Okay. So what at the biggest level, you’ve seen the extended trailer. We kinda looked at some of it. What do you think they got right? What do you think they got wrong so far? 
Larry Lawton (00:09:40) I remember some of it. The first thing that struck me right out, right in the opening when he walks up to the place. When you’re walking up to a place where the… This looks more like a trap house than it looks like a, like a jewelry, a place where they’re doing even… They’re not gonna do something with big money right in a place like this. It’s too scummy, and it’s gonna be decent, where cops aren’t gonna be there every day- 
Larry Lawton (00:10:03) … ’cause they’re gonna be there, the neighbors are gonna complain, or what are you gonna do? And then when the guy’s security here, guy’s standing there like a gun, like he’s in the Midwest. Like he’s just, gun is in his belt. And they let these two people walk in to a place. They don’t know him. They don’t know if they’re undercover cop. They don’t go with them. First thing I’m looking at saying, “What are they, crazy?” No place on the world, no gangster or no criminal on the planet is gonna let two people just walk through. “Okay, go ahead.” Unless they know you. And it confused me that whole entire trailer because it looked like Jason knew the dog. 
Larry Lawton (00:10:43) If he didn’t know the dog, that’s a hell of a bad, bad watchdog. And then the guy come in and they’re carrying guns. They’re all hanging out like they’re doing drugs sitting there. It looks more like a, you would never be manufacturing drugs there and have these kinda characters looking, sitting out front because it’s, that’s a telltale sign. You’re really calling the cops stupid, or on the take. How’s that, even better? And I think that’s gonna be part of it. 
Lex Fridman (00:11:10) So if he knows the dog, he would probably know a lot of the other people around there. 
Larry Lawton (00:11:15) Absolutely. And he would even know the area. They, he’s coming in here. He walks in. They let him in right here. And watch what happens with the dog when he walks up. He gets it. First of all, that, he had to get through two people, two, two other people to get to this door. He had to go in. One guy, then he goes to an elevator and another guy stops him. Nobody knows him. No, “Hey, I wanna see somebody.” “Okay.” No. 
Lex Fridman (00:11:39) How much of this is operating w- where everybody that works there, h- there’s like a circles of trust? How, how much is trust and loyalty and is, is, is crucial to all of this? 
Larry Lawton (00:11:51) It is supposed to be, number one, about trust. Obviously, you would not trust this many people. The cops would know this operation is happening. 
Lex Fridman (00:12:00) Look, look at the ladies in their underwear. 
Larry Lawton (00:12:02) Well, you know, actually the clothes on that, Lex, is actual normal- … for a house. I knew a bunch. I’ve been in drug houses before. Big drug houses. And what they’ll do is they’ll either be in … scrubs like a doctor’s thing and one set of clothes ’cause you don’t… One, for stealing, but I don’t even worry about stealing. It’s more about don’t have all this stuff all over you when you leave. So- 
Lex Fridman (00:12:29) Oh, so you can’t steal it or just in general? 
Larry Lawton (00:12:31) Either both. Either steal it or have it all over you and you’re gonna be pinned out in a minute. Now, obviously, look at amount of people here. There isn’t a chance they would have all these people here. This is another thing. This guy’s putting them on speaker in front of people. That’s not happening. 
Lex Fridman (00:12:49) There would be more secrecy, you’re saying. It shouldn’t, it wouldn’t be this public. 
Larry Lawton (00:12:51) Oh, there’s only… Listen, Lex, I ran a crew, and only certain people knew certain things. Nobody in my crew, nobody knew who my fence was. They mighta knew, but they can- nobody could ever have testified, “Oh, I seen this guy give Larry money.” “Oh, I’ve seen this Larry give him jewelry.” 
Lex Fridman (00:13:13) Can you explain what a fence is? 
Larry Lawton (00:13:14) A fence is a middleman. You rob something, you have to give it to somebody who can get rid of it. You have fences who can fence anything, and then in the jewelry… Here’s why people rob diamonds. There was a robbery in France at the Carlton Hotel about, oh, I don’t know, seven years ago, maybe eight years ago. I’m guessing I was on TV on that. And they robbed $140 million in diamonds in a briefcase. You couldn’t carry $140 million in bills. It’s heavy. One of the scenes in here, they’re throwing bags around like it’s like, like not even like weighing Superman. Diamonds, you could pick up 136 mil, whatever it was, and walk out in a briefcase. Now, let’s say you got 20% of that. You know, you’re still talking $25 million. You’re talking about a lot of money. How do you carry $25 million? 
Lex Fridman (00:14:15) So these guys the cops found out, so there’s supposedly here crooked cops, right? 
Larry Lawton (00:14:22) Absolutely, and there are crooked cops. I mean, I dealt with crooked cops. Listen, back in the day, in Miami day, oh, everything was crooked. I used to keep 50,000 in my trunk- … just to, in case I needed it, either to buy something or pay off cops. That’s exactly what you do. They would know it. They go, “What’s in the trunk? Go get it and let me go.” 
Lex Fridman (00:14:44) So the reality of this world is that there’s some percent of cops that are crooked. Can you speak to… Because there’s a lot of cops who are good. 
Larry Lawton (00:14:54) Absolutely. I say that as well. 
Lex Fridman (00:14:56) And that is like they’re essential to the functioning of society, and they’re, I mean, they’re… It’s one of the most, I think, valuable and dangerous jobs is being a police officer, so they deserve respect, I think. But- 
Larry Lawton (00:15:09) But hold on. I’m gonna go one-on-one with cops ’cause I train cops now. I actually taught the police academy in Missouri, where I’m an honorary cop, which- … that is wild. I mean, it’s still- 
Lex Fridman (00:15:20) Yeah, it is. 
Larry Lawton (00:15:21) I should have brought my badge. I have to give you my badge. And it’s pretty wild. It was very- It was an honor. I mean, it was a big deal. We had 13 police chiefs. They had security. It was newspapers all over the world. And the problem I have with cops is they forget that they’re part of the community and not against it. Talking about regular. You wanna go after these kinda clowns on GTA- … have at it. You wanna mess with regular people for a ticket or be a money grab, which it is, you know, cops stop someone, give ’em a ticket for bullshit. 
Larry Lawton (00:16:00) And it shouldn’t be. You create this us against them mentality. Now, I support good cops, period. If I was a police officer – honorary I am, but I can’t stop people – but if I had to be a police officer in today’s world, I would be part of the community, not against it. 
Lex Fridman (00:16:18) You would be a human being. So part of the community- 
Larry Lawton (00:16:21) First. 
Lex Fridman (00:16:21) … and if you see a friend, you would behave like a human being first. 
Larry Lawton (00:16:25) You know, I had an incident that happened, and I have- I get a lot of this ’cause I help people. Parent called a, you know, had a neighbor who was a cop, said, “Hey, my son’s having problems. Can you talk to him?” and stuff. The kid found- The guy found some paraphernalia, cocaine paraphernalia, whatever it was. You know, he arrested the kid. Come on. You’re trying to help this kid. And to see how they set it up for, it’s, it boggles the mind how they treated that man. Then they have biker gangs, obviously, the Outlaws, the Hells Angels. They’re in there too as well. But you know, you’ll find that most of the gangs, if anybody tells you they were in a medium security prison and they see the Aryan Brother, they’re not ’cause they don’t go to medium security prison. They’re all murderers. They’re all, most of them are life. If they get out on appeal, I mean, they really control the outside as well, and that’s why they were intimidating the guards too. They have a whole network on the outside. 
Larry Lawton (02:56:32) And it’s funny, Lex, because you’re gonna see them work with Black groups, or you’re gonna see them work with Mexican groups or Spanish. It doesn’t matter. You have to. You know, we… You can’t just be alone in prison, especially in prison. On the yard, they hang with themselves. They’ll play cards themselves. They’ll work out together. The MA are amazingly tight. That’s the Mexican Mafia. They will workout, sick workouts. That’s how I got into the workouts with them, and they will… And they’re doing that ready for war. I mean, they come up with that routine, and I hope you try that routine. 
Lex Fridman (02:57:07) Did you have to choose, like with all these gangs, did you have to- 
Larry Lawton (02:57:11) I got into the law. I was, you know, by being into the law so deep, I mean, I’m in the law library. I did favors for people. I had connections on the street with a lawyer so I can get people’s paperwork. So I ended up working with the shot callers for the gangs. The shot callers are the people who run the gangs. Now, when you can do that, I mean, they’d, you know, listen, they’d say, “Oh, we’ll pay you.” And, “You got me. Whatever you want. Whatever you want.” And I would… When I pull a guy’s paperwork, you know, they knew, ’cause I didn’t do this, “Oh, it’s good. Go get ’em.” I didn’t want that. Here’s what it is. This is not lying. I used to justify myself when people got messed up pretty good, and they got… 
Larry Lawton (02:57:54) I watched a guy get kicked in the head so hard with steel. Not well, I don’t know if it was steel. It was steel. But he was getting hit in the head with boots, and every time they kicked him in the head, a six-foot line of blood just went poof. And they’re kicking him and kicking. He listen, he was a real degenerate. I mean, it’s hard for me to feel any kind of pity for people who pick on a six-year-old. I mean, some people just… Life can get tough, and it should get tough for somebody like that. It shouldn’t be easy. You know, so I mean the part of me believes in tough punishment for that. But obviously I’m a believer in rehabilitation, and there is two systems, which kinda gets me a little bit upset. 
Larry Lawton (02:58:41) There’s a system for people who could afford great lawyers, and there’s a system who can’t, and that I don’t believe in. People get the wrong lawyer, and they got life in prison, and they got the right lawyer, and you’re not gonna do time. Another guy who did the exact same thing as him would be in jail. And let, just be honest with it. And you know, if you’re honest with it, if a person comes in, no argument, then I get it. I would take advantage of the system now. And that’s okay, but don’t say you’re better or they’re just a scumbag ’cause they did this, though they’re in prison. There’s a lot of good people in prison. Lot of scumbags too. 
Lex Fridman (02:59:21) There’s a lot of good people and scumbags out in the- 
Larry Lawton (02:59:24) Exactly. 
Lex Fridman (02:59:24) … outside of prison as well. 
Larry Lawton (02:59:25) Absolutely. 
Lex Fridman (02:59:27) You mentioned you might have some ideas how to fix the prison system. 
Larry Lawton (02:59:31) I have a way to fix the violence in prison and the corruption in prison very quickly for no money, zero money. First of all, the problem with prison, we all know, is everybody thinks they know what it is. It’s really the laws. We’re putting people in prison for minor bullshit. That has to stop. The best way to fix the prison system, they have a thing called the ACA. It’s called the American Accredi-creditation Association. You wanna talk bullshit, Lex? They come to a prison, and they say, “Oh, we’re an ACA-approved prison.” Really? They call them two weeks beforehand and say, “We’re gonna come inspect your prison.” You know what they do with the inmates who are bad inmates in the hole? I watch men go crazy in the hole. I mean crazy. 
Larry Lawton (03:00:16) Take feces out and write demonic stuff on the walls with feces. Throw feces and urine at people who, you know, the guards or people. Sick stuff goes on in prison because they’re going crazy, that people don’t… You can’t think this is the right way to work. Well, the way the ACA works, they’ll come to the prison, they’ll inspect the food. We loved when the AC come ’cause they’d feed us right. 
Larry Lawton (03:00:44) And things would get done. Things were fixed that were broke forever. Things happened when the ACA came. But it’s bullshit ’cause right when they left… Let me tell you, they have a prison where I live, a local jail, accredited. They have dates on the filters in the system, “Use only for inspection.” So that means when there’s no inspection, not even being filtered air. So I mean, how are we trusting these people to do anything else right? So what you could do, I could put together a team, somebody like myself, a guard, a former warden, a former medical personnel worked in it, and maybe a former administrator. We would have complete authority to go into any prison that, let’s say it’s the federal system, any prison at any time. 
Larry Lawton (03:01:35) The minute they stop us from going in, the person who stopped us is fired. He loses his pension. He loses everything. It’ll happen one time. The word will get out, “You better let these people in.” Because you know a United States senator cannot go to a prison right now and go in and inspect that? One hundred of the most powerful people, 535 congressmen and senators, 100 senators, 435 congressmen, they cannot go into any prison and inspect that prison unless they get clearance. It takes weeks. They have to be notified. That’s not an inspection. That’s bullshit. Have a team that can be put together, and that team has authority to walk into that prison at nine o’clock on a Sunday night. 
Larry Lawton (03:02:20) Now, the reason you have a person like myself, not just guards, ’cause I’m gonna know, one, how to talk to the inmates to get them to tell me the truth, ’cause they’re not gonna tell another guard ’cause they think they’re just gonna be abused. I even have a way where I could stop them from being abused by having a call-in system from the office back to them to see if they’re being abused, being transferred. Because what they do is they take that crazy inmate who’s in the hole, and you know what they do during inspection? They put him at the tier at the end, and they will literally shoot him with Thorazine and shut him up. So now, “Oh, no, we went and inspected.” If you had a person- I would know where to go. 
Larry Lawton (03:03:00) If I told you right now, “Lex, I want you and a bunch of people to go into that prison and just make sure it’s right,” you would know where to go, who to talk to, how it works. It, it would be useless. If it was just a guard, he knows that way. He doesn’t know the what’s the real p- what’s really going on with the inmates. I’m one of the only prisoners who went back to his own prison and actually spoke at a pre-release class, and it was amazing. I’m walking on the yard with the warden and the captain. I go, “This is freaking surreal.” I’m walking like no m– ’cause they have movements. You know, you can’t just move in a prison. They have what they call 10-minute moves. So they’ll say “10-minute move, 10-minute move.” So at one o’clock they say, “10-minute move,” you have 10 minutes. 
Larry Lawton (03:03:45) You leave your unit, you go wherever you’re gonna go. After the move is closed, the prison is shut down. 
Larry Lawton (03:03:50) So if you go to the yard, great, go to the yard. You can’t leave that yard till the next move. You go to the library, you can’t move that yard to… Wherever you go, education or wherever it is, you can’t leave that spot until the next move. These are called controlled moves, and they’re done for high security prisons. So that prison right now has moves. How do you move around a prison, you would move around a prison if you don’t know where to move to? How it’s set up, how the commissary works. Do you know how much money they’re making, these prisons? You know, it drove me crazy when I got out of prison. I had a transistor radio. They charged me $100 in prison. I got out of that prison, that exact radio was $9.99. 
Lex Fridman (03:04:38) How does that make sense? How do- 
Larry Lawton (03:04:40) ‘Cause they, ’cause they’re just gouging and they, they don’t realize they’re gouging the families of the people who have to try to get… Do you know what a phone call costs? You only get 300 minutes a month to use to phone call your loved ones. That’s nothing if you, if you think about it. At 300 minutes a month, and it costs you three, it, for 15 minutes costs you… It was $3.75. 
Larry Lawton (03:05:04) Think about the money you’re spending, or you’re not spending, your family is spending to give you the money. So who you hurting? There’s so many little things I could do to fix the system. The first to fix the violence would be to put together a team, a team that has authority to go into that. Now, I wouldn’t fire the warden. Maybe he really don’t know. Let’s say I go with my team into this prison. We find out there’s abuse going on here. They’re not giving them recreation. They’re not doing this, they’re not doing that. So all of that happens, right? So I would then give the warden the report. “Let’s fix this thing. We’re gonna reinspect it another time. Any questions, Warden, who we talk to, how it is, whatever?” “Nope.” We don’t tell him when we’re coming back. 
Larry Lawton (03:05:48) It could be two months, could be six months, could be whatever. 
Lex Fridman (03:05:51) I love this. 
Larry Lawton (03:05:51) And make him held accountable. 
Lex Fridman (03:05:53) Yeah, I love this. 
Larry Lawton (03:05:54) And nobody is doing it. 
Lex Fridman (03:05:54) Have you pitched this to anybody? There’s very low- 
Larry Lawton (03:05:56) You know, no. I have an actual plan where I can do for, also for recidivism to lower recidivism. Which is the rate of people coming back to prison, ’cause almost, almost two-thirds go back to prison. You know, something like 60-some, 65%. And depending on where you leave the prison system from. So there is ways to fix, besides the laws, there’s ways to literally take a prison and stop the violence, stop the abuse, ’cause usually it’s a small percentage of the guards that are abusive. You know, and they get power, and they don’t belong in the position to begin with. You know, it’s the bullying complex kind of thing. 
Lex Fridman (03:06:35) And they can do a lot of damage. Just one guard can do a lot of damage. 
Larry Lawton (03:06:38) Oh my God. And even the other guards, just like cops. I do a policing program where what I do. Cops are the same way. I mean, they, you know what- 
Lex Fridman (03:06:47) They protect each other, you mean? 
Larry Lawton (03:06:50) Put it this way. People say to me, “Well, Larry, it’s not all of them.” I said, “Let me ask you a question. If I owned a company and I have 100 employees, do I know who the screw-ups are?” I’ll eventually know who they are, and they’re fired. You don’t think out of those 100 guards, all those other people don’t know who the slacker is, who the guy who’s abusing people, who’s got a bad attitude, who’s beating people. You don’t think they know? They know. 
Larry Lawton (03:07:12) But do you think they’re gonna do anything about it? Here’s why they don’t do anything. One guard saved my life. He was a big Black guy. I wish I knew his name. I’d buy him a vacation. I was in the hole when I was going crazy, and I did things in that hole from flood it. I got beaten so much that I think I felt alive to be beaten. And he used to come to my cell, open the flat door at night. He worked at midnight the midnight shift. He would open that chute door. He would talk to me through the chute and say, you know… We’d talk about God. We’d talk about life. We’d talk about a lot of things. And he kinda put me in a better mindset for the next upcoming whatever. And he doesn’t know it, but those little talks literally saved my life from going crazy. 
Larry Lawton (03:08:02) And the compassion he had, you know, and I used to get mad, Lex. I used to get mad. “Why you know this is going on? You’re telling me at night. Why don’t you do something?” It took me until I got out of prison to realize that man is trying to raise a family, feed his own family. He can’t put himself in danger in that place because it is a violent place, and if he don’t get the backing from his guard, something can happen or he can be put on. So it took me, the mature, mature part of me to realize, “Wait a minute. He’s doing that, and he’s doing what he can instead of just, ‘Ah, fuck Lon.'” 
Lex Fridman (03:08:40) Like you said, you’re beaten, essentially tortured. What gave you strength through that, mental strength? 
Larry Lawton (03:08:48) What made me survive more than anything was I had two young kids, and I just wanted to get out and see them. You know, I really feel there’s so much to do. I love to help people. And now you gotta remember, I got out of prison at 46 years old. I went away at 34, 46. So now I get a phone call, talking to people, doing good, having fun, meeting friends again, you know, starting to adapt a little bit to society. I get a phone call from lady named Jean Bandish. She says, “Mr. Lawton, Judge Rymann would like to see you.” “I ain’t seeing no judge.” She goes, “No, she just wants to hear about certain things.” And I go, “Listen, do you have a warrant? Do you have a subpoena? ‘Cause I’m not coming to see no judge. I know the law.” So, “No,” she goes, “I think you don’t understand. 
Larry Lawton (03:09:38) She wants to hear this. She heard you talk about kids.” Still scared, thinking, what am I doing wrong? What do they want me for? I don’t trust the system. And I agreed to do it, and I don’t even know how to do anything. So I had my nephew help me, who’s since passed. A nephew helped me with a PowerPoint. What’s a Power- I didn’t know what a PowerPoint at the time was. So we make 10 slides, Lex, about a PowerPoint. And as we’re doing the PowerPoint, just slides of what I talk to the kids about. I go in on a Friday. I go into the judge’s chambers. Now, we find out years later I’m not even supposed to be back there. I’m on paper and everything. Supposed to have security with me and all that kind of stuff. Now I go to dinner with judges. A lot of them are my friends. 
Larry Lawton (03:10:26) So we sit in there, I walk in and there’s two other pe- four before them, me, I’m sitting there and, “Oh, hey, Mr. Lawton, how you doing? Thank you for coming. Can you show us what you do?” You know, they helped me put the projector. I didn’t know anything how to do that. I put it in the thing. I had a laptop and put the projector. I tell them what I do. “Thank you, Mr. Lawton. Would you like to stay for the rest of the meeting?” “No. I’m outta here.” And I literally wanna get outta there. You know, I felt ba- I mean, you know, it’s a weird feeling. I do that. I leave. It’s a Friday. Monday morning I get a phone call from Jean Bandish who says, “Hey, Mr. Lawton, I have to give you a heads up. Judge Rymann sentenced two people to your program.” What fucking program? 
Larry Lawton (03:11:11) I don’t have a program. From there, I developed the program now. We have a 90% success rate in keeping kids out of jail. We have a 70% success rate by changed attitudes from the parents. We have a 43% success rate in increased education, better grades, and a 31% increase in attendance. And I didn’t do that survey. Eastern Florida State College did that. They asked for the data and people, and they did all the calling. They have a whole thing, graphs, all that stuff. And you would know about that. 
Larry Lawton (03:11:55) Anyway, they do this data and I ended up getting recognized on the floor of Congress for helping police agencies, ’cause I also have a program where I help integrate police and stop the us against them mentality police have with, police and the communities have. You know, it’s such an us against them. So the program I developed, I was doing myself and doing… And now it’s gotten so big that we had to put it on video and now kids get sentenced with the program. They have to complete the thing, then they have to take a test and survey that they watched everything, get a certificate of completion, and give it to the court. It’s so powerful. 
Larry Lawton (03:12:34) If we had that program in Fort Lauderdale right here where Cruz killed the kids from the high school, and I lived right near, not far from that high school they woulda had, the police woulda had a tool to try to intervene and help this kid before he went crazy because, you know, they had many interactions with that kid and they never gave him a… They didn’t have anything. Even if it didn’t work, they could say they tried. We tried this program or that program. We gave it to him. We tried to help the parent and, I mean, police have a tough enough job obviously and to pick something out, but when you have that many interactions with somebody. And we even put it where it can be used for detention. 
Larry Lawton (03:13:17) Kid does something stupid in school, he has to go there, he has to watch the program, he has to pass the program. And then you could see, ’cause I do a whole survey and I could show you thousands and you could see the mindset. And if you saw a kid that said, you know, “I hate the world anyway. I might as well just shoot someone,” boy, red flag can go off. You can then get counseling into this kid, find out really where his head’s at. There’s ways to do things, again, with young people and mostly because they respect me. I’m not one of the system. Mm-hmm. I wouldn’t rat, so my credibility is right. I’m not a former drug addict, so it’s not, “Ah, I’m not gonna do drugs. He was just a drug addict and cleaned his life out.” Everybody wants to make money. 
Larry Lawton (03:13:59) Everybody wants to be somebody. And then so you take all those positives and you bring them to a kid and I have video reviews from kids that make me cry ’cause they, you know, some of them have rough lives and when you hear how they this one kid, man, it’s so powerful, starts crying on my… I mean, I want to hug the… I did actually. And he’s young, maybe 19, 20. ‘Cause we found out my program is not just for teenagers. It’s for kids 25. Kids we all know, and you’ll know this, a young man’s brain doesn’t mature till 25, a female about 23. Not my numbers, psychology numbers, and it’s true. So and you know, anybody making bad choices needs a wake-up call what could happen to them if they keep making bad choices. 
Larry Lawton (03:14:49) And then that program actually works with cards with police agencies, so they actually carry a video card. The card is actually the video. It’s like a credit card. It’s got a QR code with a code for the police. The police chief opens the message. Says, “We’d like you to watch this video. It might help your child in a trial.” The kids watch it and they- the police chief closes it by saying, “We hope this helped you. If you have any problems, please contact us.” Each cop carries them, 10 of them in their pocket. 
Larry Lawton (03:15:18) And, you know, we’re gonna push more of that. That’s where the government loved- I mean, I used to work with the Weed and Seed program. That’s a government agency which, again, funding. They take the funding away. Weed and Seed program was a program that the government gave, and they would go to a neighborhood and weed out the bad with the US attorney. This is federal now. They’d take the US attorney in that area. They’d get the drugs off the streets, get the gangs out of there, and then seed it with programs like mine. 
Larry Lawton (03:15:50) So it was Weed and Seed program. It was a very successful program. Again, funding cut that, which drives me crazy when you have a program like that with success rate. And I used to go speak at the things, and my program was vetted by the federal government, and they used it. And then I spoke in Texas, actually. In Texas, they have the International Association of Police Chiefs headquarters, and I’ve spoke there to the executive board, actually because there’s one of my mentors in the policing who gave me a badge. And that’s weird, ’cause I’m not a supporter of most police. Most police who are screw-ups don’t deserve- And I’m not gonna lose my reputation ’cause some jerk-off police chief wants to make me, you know, think he’s great. No. 
Larry Lawton (03:16:36) There’s a police department in St. Louis, in Lake St. Louis unbelievable. A guy named Mike Force. To this day we’re friends. He’s retired. Now to Nucci, I’m still an honored police there. I got the car. It all works. Maybe get me out of a ticket. I don’t know. I don’t even use it. I don’t even carry it. But they’re so positive- 
Larry Lawton (03:16:55) … ’cause they really think about how to help people, and their first thing is not arrest. It’s help. He says, “Anybody starts telling you arrest, they don’t understand the game.” It’s, “How can we help you?” You know, when I teach police academies, and I did in St. Louis, is the first thing a cop should do when they pull somebody over is not say license or registration. How about going up to the guy and saying, “Excuse me, sir, are you okay? You know, you ran that stop sign, and I’m not even gonna give you a ticket. I just wanna make sure you’re all right, because people get hit broadside, and a lot of people can get killed. Are you all right? Everything good?” “Yes, I’m…” “All right.” And what community positive. 
Larry Lawton (03:17:39) That guy goes home, tells everybody in the world how cool the cop is instead of, “License and registration. You know what you did? You blew the sign.” Who the fuck are you, kid? You know, especially as a 22-year-old cop, and I’m a 60-year-old man. I wanna strangle him. And then you have a battery to that, but they have to understand they’re part of a community, not just us against them. We’re the cops. We got the gun. 
Lex Fridman (03:18:03) And those stories travel. The good and the bad stories travel, so you gotta put your good- 
Larry Lawton (03:18:07) You- 
Lex Fridman (03:18:07) The good ones out there. 
Larry Lawton (03:18:08) … 100%. And, you know, you get enough- And that, that all happened because a friend of mine was 78, since passed, but 78, and he gets stopped. He had four people in the car going to dinner. He rolled a stop sign, and a cop comes up. “You rolled it.” He told the story to everybody I know. “You rolled it.” “What?” “License. You rolled the sign. Give me your license.” Then he came back and threw the… He said, “I can’t give you a ticket ’cause I got a call, but don’t roll it.” He told that story to every person I know, and instead of, “Sir, everything all right?” Elderly man, nice, very successful guy, just stupid. 
Lex Fridman (03:18:51) What advice would you give to young people? 
Larry Lawton (03:18:57) Make sure your word is good. That’s probably the number one thing, I think. I think- And, and it starts early. If you say something, do it. And that doesn’t mean you can’t have a mistake, and people will know you have mistakes. Own up to them. Don’t think life’s over. You know, I also tell people this, and this I think is very important. A lot of young people come up to me at 30 years old and say, “Ah, I can’t do it. I can’t make it. I, you know, I messed up.” I said, “Hold on, buddy. I was 46 years old with a record that you don’t have, and I had to get out of prison and start over. How do I do it? Perseverance, work hard, don’t give up.” You know, the people who give up either are looking for pity. I don’t believe in pity. I believe in working hard. 
Larry Lawton (03:19:49) I think people who do work hard will get a hand up by a lot of people, ’cause people like to see that. And that, to me, is the biggest. Your life’s never- And I mean that for older people. Again, 46 years old, you’re getting out of prison. Life’s not over. Find out what you love to- I love what I do. I- As you can tell. I do. I mean, I love people, and I love to talk to young people. But, you know, Nick working with me, and his energy matches mine, and that’s pretty tough. I mean, I just have a lot of energy. Listen, when it’s all over, the lights are out, I’ll have plenty of time to rest. You know? 
Lex Fridman (03:20:27) I agree. So make sure your word is good and then work your ass off. 
Larry Lawton (03:20:32) And never quit. 
Lex Fridman (03:20:33) Never quit. Larry, you’re an incredible human being. 
Larry Lawton (03:20:37) Thank you for having me. I really appreciate that, you know? And thank you- 
Lex Fridman (03:20:40) You better be a character in a Grand Theft Auto game. I’ll put my vote in. Thank you, Larry. 
Larry Lawton (03:20:45) Thank you very much. 
Lex Fridman (03:20:47) Thanks for listening to this conversation with Larry Lawton. To support this podcast, please check out our sponsors in the description, where you can also find links to contact me, ask questions, give feedback, and so on. podcasts.title: The Missing Layer for Personal AI | First Person Labs’ Ken Liu
podcasts.description:
AI agents are getting smarter, but every new agent still has to learn who you are. What if your preferences, priorities, relationships, and digital context could move with you instead?

First Person Labs co-founder Ken Liu joins a16z’s Martin Casado and Joel de la Garza to introduce Second, a personal context layer designed to understand what you’re doing across your digital life and make that context available to the agents you choose.

They discuss how Second can proactively connect information across conversations and applications, why protecting such personal data requires a different security architecture, and the longer-term vision of AI that doesn’t just respond to prompts, but understands enough context to know when and how to help.

GPT-6.2 Astra, the #2 Frontier Model is better and 20%-600% cheaper, but has mixed reviews; 6.2 Sol likely main workhorse 
November 17, 2026 — GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol lower benchmark costs. Early testers disagree on what Astra is like to work with. 
swyx .ai 
Nov 18 · 7 min read
OpenAI shipped GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol today, two days before Anthropic’s expected first trading day . In Artificial Analysis ’ tests, Sol ties September’s Astra at about 15% of the cost per task . New Astra scores 62 on the Intelligence Index, just behind Fable 5.2 at 65. Net net, Anthropic still owns the world’s best model, but OpenAI owns the world’s most efficient models in terms of intelligence per $. 
What’s more unusual about this launch is the STRONGLY negative influencer feedback… 
Play video 
Open video on YouTube ↗ 
Play video 
Open video on YouTube ↗ 
which prompted a defensive response … 
View post on X ↗ 
We think that some of this is overreacting and normal influencer tendency to either have everything be 🤯🤯🤯 or the literal WORST.MODEL.EVER, BUT also that some of the criticisms are valid, and the RL artefacts are noticeable and downright bizarre (don’t even get us started about the terrible launch video ). However, we still use it to automate our work and that’s all that matters in the end. 
Great ship, but Anthropic’s IPO is unaffected and that will be probably the headline of the week/year/decade (until OpenAI IPO’s….)
